slides.title: File formats
slides.text: Session 1 File formats Name the dialect settings a delimited file needs: delimiter, quoting, encoding, line ending Explain how columnar files store types, compress columns and read only what a query needs Measure size, read time and type fidelity of one dataset in three formats 01

slides.title: Charging sessions reach the data team in four shapes
slides.text: The case Charging sessions reach the data team in four shapes Charger logs Text files from Vendor A and Vendor B chargers, one line per session. Legacy exports The station team's old asset system: registers and notes in Arabic. Platform API The charge-point platform's pages of nested JSON. Analysts' tables What finance and operations read: typed, partitioned, checked. The charging network runs 40 fictional stations in one unnamed city. Every file in this course is synthetic.

slides.title: A format decides what survives the trip
slides.text: What a format promises A format decides what survives the trip Promise Delimited (CSV) JSON Lines Columnar (Parquet) Types travel with the data No: all text A few: string, number, true/false, null Yes, in the file's schema Nested values No Yes Yes Append one record Yes Yes, one line No: write a new file Read only some columns No No Yes Readable in a text editor Yes Yes No

slides.title: A CSV without its dialect is half a file
slides.text: Delimited files A CSV without its dialect is half a file staff_code;grade;allowance;note 0042;B2;1250,50;"ترقية، ""مؤقتة""" 0107;A1;980,00; Delimiter: here a semicolon, because the comma is the decimal mark. Quoting: a field holding the delimiter or a quote is enclosed in quotes; an inner quote is doubled. Encoding, line ending: not in the file; someone must say them. Types: not in the file: "0042" is a code, not 42. What goes wrong. A reader with the default dialect splits the note at its comma and turns the staff code into the number 42.

slides.title: JSON Lines is one record per line, and that changes everything operational
slides.text: JSON and JSON Lines JSON Lines is one record per line, and that changes everything operational One JSON document An array of a million objects: one opening bracket, one closing bracket. To add a record, rewrite the file. A cut at byte 900,000 makes the whole file invalid. JSON Lines One complete JSON value per line, UTF-8, a newline after each. Append a line; stream it line by line; a damaged line loses one record, not the file. Still text. Every line repeats every key, and numbers and times are written as text: large on disk, and a reader must parse each value back.

slides.title: A columnar file stores each column together, typed and compressed
slides.text: Columnar files A columnar file stores each column together, typed and compressed File a footer with the schema and where everything is → Row groups blocks of rows, e.g. 100,000 sessions each → Column chunks one per column per row group, with min and max → Pages encoded and compressed values A query that needs two columns reads two chunks per row group, not every byte. Statistics let a reader skip row groups whose range cannot match. Similar values side by side compress well: codes, dates, small numbers.

slides.title: A partition is a folder per value, so a reader opens only what it needs
slides.text: Partitions A partition is a folder per value, so a reader opens only what it needs day=2026-10-19/part-0.parquet day=2026-10-20/part-0.parquet day=2026-10-21/part-0.parquet ... The value lives in the folder name (the "hive" style), not inside the files. A query for one day reads one folder. Choose a column people filter on, with tens to hundreds of values, not millions. What goes wrong. Partitioning by session id writes one tiny file per session: thousands of files and slower reads.

slides.title: Arrow lets two tools share a table in memory, with no file between them
slides.text: In memory Arrow lets two tools share a table in memory, with no file between them import duckdb, pyarrow.parquet as pq loans = pq.read_table("loans.parquet", columns=["branch", "items"]) duckdb.sql("""SELECT branch, sum(items) FROM loans GROUP BY branch""") Arrow is a columnar layout in memory, as Parquet is on disk. DuckDB finds the Python variable loans and queries it as a table. No CSV in between: the types arrive as they left.

slides.title: Compare formats on three measures, taken the same way
slides.text: Measuring Compare formats on three measures, taken the same way Size Bytes on disk. Stable: the same data gives the same size. Read time The median of several reads on one machine. It moves with the machine, the cache and the run. Type fidelity Column by column: same type and same values after a round trip with default readers. What goes wrong. One timing quoted as a property of a format. Report the machine and the median, and trust sizes and fidelity more than seconds.

slides.title: Which hand-over keeps the codes intact?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which hand-over keeps the codes intact? A library sends loan records with branch codes like "007" to analysts who read files with default settings. Which hand-over keeps "007" as "007"? A CSV with every field in quotes A Parquet file with the code declared as a string A JSON Lines file read back with the default reader settings A semicolon-separated file in UTF-8

slides.text: Debrief of lab 1.1 Parquet kept 11 of 11 columns; CSV kept 7, JSON Lines 6 Format Size Median read Lost with default readers CSV 16,894 KB 0.030 s connector, started_at, status, idle_min JSON Lines 45,219 KB 1.149 s connector, energy_kwh, amount, status, idle_min Parquet (zstd) 2,562 KB 0.016 s none The course's reference run: 200,000 synthetic sessions on one laptop. slides.title: Text and time
slides.text: Session 2 Text and time Tell bytes from characters and read a file’s first bytes for its encoding Recognise the symptom of a wrong code page, a byte order mark, double encoding and UTF-16 Convert local times without offsets to UTC, across a daylight-saving change 02

slides.title: A file holds bytes; text is bytes plus an agreed encoding
slides.text: Bytes and characters A file holds bytes; text is bytes plus an agreed encoding The word سلام in Bytes Per letter UTF-8 d8 b3 d9 84 d8 a7 d9 85 2 Windows-1256 (cp1256) d3 e1 c7 e3 1 ISO-8859-6 d3 e4 c7 e5 1 UTF-16 (little-endian, with its mark) ff fe 33 06 44 06 and so on 2

slides.title: Read a legacy file as UTF-8 and it fails; read UTF-8 as legacy and it lies
slides.text: Legacy Arabic code pages Read a legacy file as UTF-8 and it fails; read UTF-8 as legacy and it lies cp1256 bytes read as UTF-8 A UTF-8 decoder meets single high bytes it cannot use: an error, or ���� with errors="replace". Loud, at least. UTF-8 bytes read as cp1256 cp1256 maps every byte to a character, so it never fails: سلام reads as ط³ظ„ط§ظ…. Quiet, and wrong. Saved again, it sticks. Write that wrong text back as UTF-8 and the file is now double-encoded: valid UTF-8, nonsense Arabic. Undo it by reversing the wrong step: encode as cp1256, decode as UTF-8.

slides.title: A byte order mark is invisible text at the start of a file
slides.text: Byte order marks A byte order mark is invisible text at the start of a file ef bb bf: the UTF-8 mark, added by some editors and spreadsheet exports. ff fe or fe ff: the UTF-16 marks, which say the byte order. Read as plain UTF-8, the mark becomes the character glued to the first column name. df = pd.read_csv("grades.csv") df["student_code"] # KeyError df.columns[0] # ' student_code' pd.read_csv("grades.csv", encoding="utf-8-sig")

slides.title: Detection is a guess; confirm it with a word you know
slides.text: Diagnosis Detection is a guess; confirm it with a word you know 1 · Look the first bytes in hex: a mark, zero bytes, single high bytes → 2 · Try decode with the likely encoding → 3 · Confirm a value you know must appear, such as a station or branch name → 4 · Record the encoding in the load log Rule. "It opened without an error" proves nothing for a single-byte code page: every byte decodes to something.

slides.title: A time without an offset is a guess about someone's clock
slides.text: Offsets and UTC A time without an offset is a guess about someone's clock Written as Means 2026-11-02T09:00:00+03:00 09:00 on a clock three hours ahead of UTC 2026-11-02T06:00:00Z The same instant, in UTC 2026-11-02 09:00 Unknown: which clock? RFC 3339 times carry Z or +hh:mm: the instant is fixed. Store instants in UTC, keep the offset when it matters, convert to local time only to display.

slides.title: Daylight saving skips one hour in spring and repeats one in autumn
slides.text: Daylight saving Daylight saving skips one hour in spring and repeats one in autumn Spring: a missing hour In the CET zone, on 29 March 2026, clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00. A log line at 02:30 names a time that never happened there. Autumn: a repeated hour In the EET zone, on 26 October 2025, 03:30 happens twice: first at 00:30 UTC, then at 01:30 UTC. In Python. zoneinfo marks the second pass of a repeated time with fold=1. Without another clue, such as the order of events, nobody can tell which pass a bare time meant.

slides.title: Each fault leaves its own fingerprint
slides.text: From symptom to cause Each fault leaves its own fingerprint You see Look for A decode error, or � in place of Arabic A single-byte code page read as UTF-8 Arabic that reads as pairs of other Arabic letters, no error Double encoding A KeyError on a column you can see A byte order mark A zero byte after every ASCII letter UTF-16 Every time off by the same hours A fixed-offset clock read as another An offset that changes with the date A zone with daylight saving

slides.title: What happened to the catalogue file?
slides.text: Checkpoint What happened to the catalogue file? A public library's catalogue export opens in UTF-8 without any error, but its Arabic titles read as long runs of pairs like ط§ظ„. What happened? It is in cp1256 and was read as UTF-8 It starts with a UTF-8 byte order mark It was decoded as cp1256 once and saved again as UTF-8 It was saved as UTF-16

slides.text: Lab 1.2 · 90 min Six damaged files Six files from the station team and two charger vendors diagnosed from their bytes and times, repaired, checked against the platform and logged D1_2_damaged_files.ipynb Run the setup cell and look at the six files as bytes 10 min Write the diagnosis sheet before any repair 20 min Repair the four text files 25 min Convert Vendor A’s times to UTC 10 min Convert Vendor B’s times to UTC across the clock change 15 min Check against the platform and write the repair log 10 min ✱ Stretch: Guess the code page of a file without being told

slides.title: Vendor A was always 180 minutes off; Vendor B 120, then 60
slides.text: Debrief of lab 1.2 Vendor A was always 180 minutes off; Vendor B 120, then 60 A constant gap is a fixed-offset clock: localise to +03:00, convert to UTC. A gap that changes on 25 October is a zone with daylight saving. Two of Vendor B's sessions ended before they started until the repeated hour was resolved by seq. The repair log One line per file: symptom, cause, repair, rows. A repair nobody can see is a new fault.

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Day 1 · Wrap-up Three things to keep Formats carry promises Only a format with a schema carries types; the others leave them to the reader's guess. Bytes need an agreement Look at the bytes, decode, confirm with a known word, log the encoding. Times need an offset Store UTC; a bare local time is a guess, and daylight saving makes it a bad one.

slides.title: Which fault is this?
slides.text: Review of Day 1 Which fault is this? A water utility's meter readings, logged without offsets, run exactly 240 minutes ahead of the billing system's UTC times on every day of the year. What is the fault? A clock in a zone that has daylight saving time A file saved in a legacy code page A CSV that lost the column's type A clock on a fixed offset, read as UTC

slides.title: Interfaces
slides.text: Session 1 Interfaces Decide from a status code whether to retry, wait or stop Explain why cursor pagination survives inserts that offset pagination does not Build a rerunnable pull with raw responses, a checkpoint and idempotent writes 01

slides.title: A request names what you want; the status says what happened
slides.text: HTTP in one slide A request names what you want; the status says what happened request GET /v1/stations?limit=50&cursor=Yz0x with Authorization: Bearer ... status 200 OK headers Content-Type: application/json body {"data": [...50 items...], "next_cursor": "Yz01MA"} Read the status before the body: a 429 or a 500 may carry an HTML page, not your JSON.

slides.title: Each status asks the client for a different action
slides.text: Status codes Each status asks the client for a different action Status Means The client 200 Here is the data Uses it 400 401 403 404 The request is wrong or not allowed Stops and reports: repeating will not help 429 Too many requests Waits as long as Retry-After says, then repeats 500 502 503 504 The server failed, often briefly Waits longer each time, then repeats; gives up after a few tries

slides.title: An offset is a position; a cursor is a bookmark
slides.text: Pagination An offset is a position; a cursor is a bookmark Offset: "skip 100, give me 100" Newest first, five new items arrive after page 1. Every older item moves down five places, so page 2 starts with five items you already have, and the five new ones are never seen in this pull. Cursor: "after the last one I saw" The server returns an opaque token naming the last item. New items at the top do not move what comes after it; the next run picks them up. What goes wrong. Offset paging fails silently: no error, just repeats and gaps that a count by id would reveal.

slides.title: Back off exponentially, add jitter, and stop after a few tries
slides.text: Retries Back off exponentially, add jitter, and stop after a few tries Try 1 0.5 s Try 2 1 s Try 3 2 s Try 4 4 s Try 5 8 s Wait = base × 2try − 1, capped, plus a small random jitter. Jitter spreads clients that failed together, so they do not return together. A 429 with Retry-After overrides the formula.

slides.title: Keep every raw response before you parse it
slides.text: Raw responses Keep every raw response before you parse it Replay Fix a parsing bug and rerun from the saved pages, without calling the API again. Audit Show what the source said on the day, not what your code made of it. Debug An odd value downstream can be traced to the page it came from. Never the headers. Save the path, the parameters, the status and the body. The request headers carry the token.

slides.title: Write records by key, then the checkpoint: a crash anywhere is safe
slides.text: Rerunnable loads Write records by key, then the checkpoint: a crash anywhere is safe 1 · Fetch the page after the saved cursor → 2 · Save raw the page as it came → 3 · Write by id skip ids already kept → 4 · Checkpoint the next cursor A crash before step 4 means the page is fetched again; step 3 makes that harmless. "Exactly once" is proven by counting: records equal unique ids equal the source's count.

slides.title: A token belongs to a person and the environment, never to the code
slides.text: Tokens A token belongs to a person and the environment, never to the code import os # set in the shell, or in .env (excluded by .gitignore) token = os.environ["SOURCE_API_TOKEN"] auth = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"} client = httpx.Client(headers=auth) Commit .env.example with a placeholder value; never .env. A token pasted in a notebook stays in its history and every copy. Tokens are issued per person by the data's owner, who can revoke them.

slides.title: Read the terms and limits before the first request
slides.text: Respectful collection Read the terms and limits before the first request Rate limits: stay under them; honour 429 and Retry-After. Licence: what you may keep, share and publish, and how to credit the source. Retention: how long raw responses may be kept. No published limit is not permission: set your own pace, write it in the code, and say it is yours. In the lab. The public API task reads the series' licence from its metadata and stops unless it is open; it then paces itself at one request a second, the course's own rule.

slides.title: The Open Data Policy asks for machine-readable formats and a licence
slides.text: National reference The Open Data Policy asks for machine-readable formats and a licence Principle 2 · Open Format and Machine-Readable «المبدأ الثاني: الصيغة المفتوحة وإمكانية القراءة آلياً»: data is made available in a machine-readable format that allows automated processing, in widely used file formats such as CSV, XLS, JSON and XML. Principle 7 · Open Data Licensing in KSA «المبدأ السابع: ترخيص البيانات المفتوحة في المملكة»: open data is subject to a licence that sets the conditions of use; using the data indicates acceptance of the licence terms. NDMO Open Data Policy, National Data Governance Policies, version 1 of 5/5/2020, read from the PDF on sdaia.gov.sa on 25 November 2026. Paraphrased; the Arabic headings are quoted.

slides.title: Which response should the client retry?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which response should the client retry? A pull from a weather-station network's API gets these four answers on different pages. Which one should it retry after a wait, with no change to the request? 503 Service Unavailable 400 Bad Request: "limit must be at most 200" 401 Unauthorized 404 Not Found for one station

slides.title: Schema and validation
slides.text: Session 2 Schema and validation Flatten nested records into one table per grain, keys carried down Declare a schema and prove the written files match it Decide per batch whether to load, quarantine rows or reject, and report why 02

slides.title: Nested JSON becomes one table per grain, with the key carried down
slides.text: Flattening Nested JSON becomes one table per grain, with the key carried down {"visit_id": "V-0193", "clinic": {"id": "C04", "floor": 2}, "booked_at": "2026-11-03T08:40:00+03:00", "tests": [{"code": "T-11", "result": 5.4}, {"code": "T-27", "result": 0.9}]} Once per visit (the clinic object): columns of the visits table, clinic_id, clinic_floor. A list (the tests): its own table, one row per test, with visit_id on every row. Count after flattening: visits equal records; tests equal the sum of list lengths.

slides.title: Declare the schema in code, and cast to it before writing
slides.text: Declared types Declare the schema in code, and cast to it before writing import pyarrow as pa VISITS = pa.schema([ pa.field("visit_id", pa.string(), nullable=False), pa.field("clinic_id", pa.string(), nullable=False), pa.field("booked_at", pa.timestamp("us", tz="UTC"), nullable=False), pa.field("month", pa.string(), nullable=False), # the partition column ]) table = pa.Table.from_pandas(visits, schema=VISITS, preserve_index=False) A value that cannot be cast fails here, at the boundary, not in next month's report.

slides.title: Prove the files match the declaration by reading their schema back
slides.text: Proof Prove the files match the declaration by reading their schema back 1 · Write partitioned by the declared column → 2 · Read the schema of one written file → 3 · Compare with the declaration, minus the partition column → 4 · Count rows read back from the whole folder Why minus one column. In hive partitioning the partition value lives in the folder name; readers add it back as a column.

slides.title: Check each record, then check the table
slides.text: Validation Check each record, then check the table Layer Rules Example tool Record , one at a time Required fields, types, patterns (a time with its offset), allowed values JSON Schema Table , the batch as a whole Unique keys, ranges, one column against another, values that must exist in a register Pandera Record checks run before flattening, on the raw JSON. Table checks run on the typed table, after the cast.

slides.title: A JSON Schema states what one record must be
slides.text: Record checks A JSON Schema states what one record must be {"type": "object", "required": ["visit_id", "clinic", "booked_at", "tests"], "properties": { "visit_id": {"type": "string", "pattern": "^V-[0-9]{4}$"}, "booked_at": {"type": "string", "pattern": "^[0-9-]{10}T[0-9:]{8}(Z|[+-][0-9]{2}:[0-9]{2})$"}, "tests": {"type": "array", "minItems": 1}}} Each error names its rule (required, type, pattern) and its path: the report's reason.

slides.title: Named table checks give every failing row a reason
slides.text: Table checks Named table checks give every failing row a reason import pandera.pandas as pa checks = pa.DataFrameSchema( {"visit_id": pa.Column(None, pa.Check(lambda s: ~s.duplicated(keep=False), name="duplicate_key")), "clinic_id": pa.Column(None, pa.Check(lambda s: s.isin(CLINICS), name="unknown_clinic"))}, checks=[pa.Check(lambda df: df["seen_at"] >= df["booked_at"], name="seen_before_booked")]) checks.validate(visits, lazy=True) # raises SchemaErrors listing every failure

slides.title: Reject the batch, or quarantine rows: decide by written rules
slides.text: The decision Reject the batch, or quarantine rows: decide by written rules The interface changed a required field missing from nearly every record: reject the batch, name the field ↓ Some rows break the rules quarantine each with its reason, keep the rest ↓ Too many rows break above the organisation's threshold: reject the batch ↓ Otherwise load the valid rows

slides.title: Quarantine so that owners see what failed, and fix it at the source
slides.text: Quarantine Quarantine so that owners see what failed, and fix it at the source The loader Writes each row with its rule and meaning; does not edit or release rows. The data owner Corrects the source and sends the rows again. A second person Reviews any release of quarantined rows. Next. Data contracts, with versions and service levels between sender and receiver, follow in DEV-DAT-204.

slides.title: Load, quarantine or reject?
slides.text: Checkpoint Load, quarantine or reject? A library's loans batch has 400 rows. Twelve rows (3%) name a branch code that is not in the branch register; every other check passes. The written rules: reject on a changed interface, or above 5% quarantined. Reject the whole batch Map the twelve codes to the nearest valid branch and load all Load 388 rows and quarantine 12 with their reason Load 388 rows and drop the 12

slides.title: Your follow-up task: a checked ingestion script, run live on an unseen batch
slides.text: The capstone Your follow-up task: a checked ingestion script, run live on an unseen batch One script: read the register in its real encoding, convert a vendor log to UTC, validate the sessions, write typed Parquet, quarantine and report. Practise on labs/capstone/practice/ and on batches of your own seeds. Hand in a public GitHub repository link within two weeks; no token or .env in it. On the day The assessor generates a batch you have not seen. You run the script live for six minutes, then answer five minutes of questions.

slides.title: A checked ingestion script, run live on a batch you have not seen
slides.text: What was asked A checked ingestion script, run live on a batch you have not seen Reads the register in its real encoding and proves it. Converts the vendor log to UTC, the repeated hour included. Checks every session record and the table rules; loads, quarantines or rejects by stated rules. Writes typed Parquet partitioned by day, a quarantine file and a report. Gives the same files when run twice. Submitted A public GitHub repository link within two weeks of the workshop: script, schemas, README, a practice run's report. No token, key or .env file.

slides.title: Six criteria, 100 points
slides.text: How the capstone is scored Six criteria, 100 points Inputs read right, repairs logged 20 Output matches the declared schema 15 Checks with stated rules 20 Rerunnable, input untouched 10 A report the owner can act on 10 Live run, decided and explained 25 In the course: labs 40%, check 20%, script and report 30%, live run 10%. Pass: 70%, with the batch decided for the right reasons.

Run the script on it, open the report, say what it decided and why. 5 min · questions The assessor asks about one decision, one repair and one rule, from the key in front of them. 2 min · changeover The next participant shares their screen and opens a terminal.
